Thank you, Plácido, that was very clear. Can I start the Q&A session with a hypothetical question?
Of course, Megan. Go ahead.
If we offered you a two-year contract, would you buy more from us than from your other suppliers?
Probably, yes. But it would depend on the lead time. If the lead time were shorter than ten weeks, I would move more of my orders to you.
Interesting. Could you elaborate a little? How much more?
Off the top of my head, about thirty percent more. I can give you a ballpark figure now and the exact numbers next week.
That works. And if the price of aluminum went up next year, would you still sign?
If I were you, I would put that in the contract. It is always a trade-off: a fixed price or a reliable delivery. Let me get back to you on that by Friday.

Thank you, that was a very useful presentation. I've got three quick questions, if that's all right. First, before we placed any order, we would need the full spec sheet, with the alloy and the thickness of every product. Could you send that? Second, volume. If we doubled our order next year, could your company scale up in time, or would the lead time get longer? And third, the price. I know it's difficult to say now, but if you could give me a ballpark figure by the end of the week, that would help a lot. I don't need the exact number today. Thanks very much.

That's a good question, and I'll be honest with you. If you ordered every month instead of every quarter, we could plan our production much better, and your lead time would go down from twelve weeks to about eight. That is the trade-off for us: regular orders, faster delivery. About the price, I'm afraid I can't give you a fixed price for two years. The price of aluminum changes every day on the market, and if we promised a fixed price, we would be taking a very big risk. What I can offer is a fixed price for six months, and then a review. If I were you, I would accept that. It's what most of our clients in Europe do.

Here's something I see all the time. People spend three weeks on their slides and three minutes thinking about the questions. And then the Q&A session starts, and that's where the deal is really made or lost. My advice? Write down the ten questions you'd hate to get, and prepare them. And if somebody asks you something you really don't know, don't invent a number. Just say: that's a great question, let me check and get back to you by Thursday. People respect that. Oh, and one more thing. When the audience starts asking what-if questions, if we did this, would you do that, relax. That's a good sign. It means they're already imagining the deal.
